lesson.title: Stripping Away the Baseline: The AC Component
lesson.summary: The AC component of a signal is everything left over after subtracting its DC component, the time-varying part that swings above and below the average.
lesson.body:
Once the DC component a0 has been identified, the AC component is defined simply as whatever remains: f_AC(t) = f(t) - a0, which equals the sum over n = 1, 2, 3, ... of [an cos(n omega0 t) + bn sin(n omega0 t)]. This connects directly to the Alternating Current prerequisite: by construction, this remainder always has an average value of exactly zero over one period, since every individual cosine and sine term integrates to zero over a full period on its own. Subtracting the DC component from any periodic signal is guaranteed to leave behind something that genuinely alternates around zero, never around some other offset.

This split matters because real components and instruments are often built to respond to only one piece or the other. A series coupling capacitor passes the AC component while blocking the DC component, which is exactly why capacitors are used between amplifier stages to remove an unwanted DC bias while preserving the signal. An AC voltmeter is built to read only the AC component and ignore any DC present. In a power supply, the AC component riding on top of the intended DC output is called ripple, and a major design goal is to make its amplitude as small as possible relative to the DC level.

Here is a fully worked example, continuing directly from the PWM pulse train in the DC Component chapter: v(t) sits at 5 V for 2 ms and 0 V for 8 ms of every 10 ms period, with a verified DC component of 1 V. The AC component is v(t) - 1 V: during the 2 ms on-time, the AC component equals 5 - 1 = 4 V; during the 8 ms off-time, it equals 0 - 1 = -1 V. Check that this new waveform really does average to zero, as required: (4 V times 2 ms + (-1 V) times 8 ms) / 10 ms = (8 - 8)/10 ms = 0 V, confirmed. So the AC component is itself a fully valid periodic waveform, an asymmetric pulse swinging between +4 V and -1 V, that by construction always averages to zero, while the original combined signal swings between 0 V and 5 V and averages to 1 V.

Put together, DC component plus AC component is just another name for a0 plus every an and bn term combined, which is another way of stating what a Fourier series already says: every well behaved periodic signal decomposes exactly, with nothing left over and nothing approximated, into a constant baseline and a purely alternating remainder riding on top of it.
